title: Event-driven architectures (EDAs) are a great choice for many use cases. | Darryl R.
content: Darryl R. 7mo Report this post Event-driven architectures (EDAs) are a great choice for many use cases. They can be difficult to design and are more complicated to test but they can work really well - especially in the public cloud where you have elastic resource availability. An example is below. Order processing systems are examples where EDAs typically can shine. Using managed AWS services like AWS Lambda for business logic, EventBridge as the event bus, SQS for resilience, and DynamoDB tables for isolated data storage is common. Asim provides a detailed walk through of all the components in an EDA architecture on AWS. If you want to see an example to get started check this out. https://lnkd.in/ed3HPHWw Decoupling at Scale: My Deep Dive into AWS Event-Driven Architecture (API Gateway, EventBridge, SQS) dev.to 26 1 Comment Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X Eduardo Bertrand 7mo Report this comment This is an impressive and thorough breakdown, Darryl! It’s a great example of how event-driven architectures can bring decoupling, resilience, and scalability to complex systems like e-commerce order processing. I especially appreciate how you highlighted: Using EventBridge as the central bus to decouple services and enable independent evolution. Leveraging SQS with DLQs for reliable asynchronous processing. Implementing CloudFormation YAML IaC to gain low-level, hands-on insight into AWS resource relationships. The practical application of KMS CMKs for encryption and operational best practices. Your point about EDA being particularly effective in the cloud where resources are elastic really resonates. It’s not just about architecture elegance but operational practicality.
